lesson.title: Maritime Empires Established
lesson.summary: How European states built trading-post empires, joint-stock companies, and colonies, and how some African and Asian states grew through new trade.
learningGoals: Explain the process of state building and expansion among maritime empires from 1450 to 1750.
Explain how joint-stock companies and trading posts operated.
Explain how African states such as Kongo and Asante took part in new trade networks.
lesson.bigIdea: European maritime empires grew through fortified trading posts, chartered companies, and conquest, while some African and Asian states used new trade to grow stronger.
lesson.context: Once sea routes were known, European states and merchants competed to control them. Their methods ranged from naval force at Asian ports to conquest of entire American empires.

sections.title: Trading-post empires

blocks.text: Portugal seized fortified ports such as Goa in 1510 and Malacca in 1511. It required Asian ships to buy passes and pay duties, enforcing the system with armed ships.
Most Indian Ocean trade remained in Asian hands, and land empires such as the Mughals were barely affected. A trading-post empire controlled points on the coast, not whole regions.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Do not describe Portugal as ruling India. It held a handful of coastal forts while powerful Asian states ruled the interior.

sections.takeaway: Trading-post empires used naval force to profit from trade without governing large territories.

sections.title: Joint-stock companies

blocks.text: The English East India Company, chartered in 1600, and the Dutch East India Company, or VOC, chartered in 1602, raised money by selling shares to investors. These joint-stock companies spread the risk of long voyages among many owners.
Governments gave the companies the right to build forts, keep armies, and make treaties. The VOC, based at Batavia on Java from 1619, used force to control the spice trade.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: Long voyages were costly and risky, so merchants pooled money in joint-stock companies, which let them fund fleets and armies and compete for control of Asian trade.

sections.takeaway: Joint-stock companies combined private investment with state-like powers.

sections.title: Conquest in the Americas

blocks.text: Hernán Cortés, with tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, defeated the Mexica between 1519 and 1521. Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532 during a civil war within the empire.

Spain built a land empire in the Americas with viceroys, colonial courts, and the Catholic Church. Portugal colonized Brazil, while France, England, and the Netherlands founded colonies in North America and the Caribbean.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: A small number of Spanish soldiers did not conquer the Mexica alone. Indigenous allies, disease, and internal divisions were essential.

sections.takeaway: In the Americas, Europeans built territorial empires rather than trading posts.

sections.title: African states and Atlantic trade

blocks.text: The Kingdom of Kongo established ties with Portugal in the 1480s. King Afonso I adopted Christianity but protested Portuguese slave raiding. The Asante kingdom, rising around 1700, sold gold and enslaved war captives to Europeans for firearms and cloth.
European traders on the West African coast generally depended on African rulers and merchants, who controlled access to the interior.

sections.takeaway: Some African states grew stronger by taking part in Atlantic trade, including the slave trade.

vocabulary.definition: An empire that controlled trade through fortified coastal ports rather than by ruling large territories.
Businesses that raised money by selling shares to investors, who shared profits and risks; some held state-like powers.
The Dutch East India Company, a joint-stock company chartered in 1602 that controlled much of the spice trade.
A west-central African kingdom whose rulers adopted Christianity and traded with Portugal from the late 1400s.
A West African kingdom that rose around 1700 and grew powerful through trade in gold and enslaved captives.

connections.title: Land and sea empires
connections.body: The Ottomans, Safavids, and Mughals expanded over land, while Portugal and the Netherlands built empires of ports and sea lanes.
connections.transferQuestion: Explain one difference between a land-based empire and a trading-post empire.
connections.feedback: Name an example of each and explain how each controlled territory or trade.
